design_detail: Systematic review with narrative synthesis (no meta-analysis), reported as guided by PRISMA, of general-population prospective cohort studies in which the age of first drink (AFD; more than a few sips) was measured in adolescence at least 3 years before alcohol outcomes at 18 or older. Medline, Embase, PsycInfo and Social Policy and Practice were searched from inception to 10 January 2013, with citation searching and expert contact. Five reports from four cohorts (two US, two Norwegian; n 447 to 1311) were included; risk of bias and confounding were appraised narratively.
can_establish: What the prospective general-population cohort literature up to January 2013 showed about whether an earlier first drink, measured in adolescence, goes with adult drinking and alcohol problems, and how the reported associations changed with adjustment for confounders.
cannot_establish: Whether delaying the first drink would reduce adult alcohol problems (every included study is observational and none controls for unmeasured familial factors); a pooled size of any association (no meta-analysis); anything about drugs other than alcohol or about countries outside the USA and Norway; or the effects of first intoxication or of early regular drinking, which were excluded as exposures.

sample.recruitment: Database search of Medline, Embase, PsycInfo and Social Policy and Practice from inception to 10 January 2013, without language or date restrictions but limited to peer-reviewed studies; backward searching of reference lists and forward citation searching of included studies; 20 experts on young people's drinking contacted; the references of a related review (McCambridge, McAlaney & Rowe, 2011) screened (Methods, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Box 1 gives the PsycInfo strategy). The included cohorts were school-based (Oslo; Seattle; a national Norwegian school cohort) or community-based (Rutgers Health and Human Development Project, USA) (Results, 1st paragraph; Table 1).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: general-population cohort studies; AFD defined as a first drink of more than a few sips (studies measuring only first intoxication or the start of regular drinking were excluded); AFD measured in adolescence with at least 3 years between the initial AFD measurement and the outcome; outcomes at 18 or older (consumption, DSM- or ICD-defined dependence or non-dependent problems, or other harmful use such as fights while drinking); a reported magnitude of association; peer-reviewed. Excluded: special populations such as children of alcoholics; cross-sectional and case-control studies, because of recall and reporting bias in retrospective AFD (Methods, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
sample.demographics: Included cohorts (Table 1): Pedersen & Skrondal 1998, Oslo school cohort, n=522, follow-up 89%, AFD charted at five waves from 12–15 to 18–21, outcomes at 18–21; Warner & White 2003, Rutgers project, n=447, 83%, AFD at 12, 15 and 18, outcomes to 30–31; Guttmannova et al. 2011, Seattle Social Development Project, n=808, 92%, AFD in four bands up to 18–20, outcomes every three years from 21 to 33; Guttmannova et al. 2012, same cohort, subset of 706, AFD before 11 or not; Rossow & Kuntsche 2013, Young in Norway, n=1311, 82.4%, any drinking by 13–14, one outcome wave at 26–27. Sex and other participant characteristics are not tabulated. No study came from a low- or middle-income country or a Mediterranean culture (Discussion, 5th paragraph).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level. Follow-up in the included cohorts was 82.4% to 100% (Table 1); the Warner & White sample was restricted to people who provided data at every wave, and the 100% given for the Seattle 2012 report describes an analytic subset (706 of the cohort's 808 in the 2011 report).
sample.selection_effects: Only five reports from four cohorts met the criteria, three of them (2011 to 2013) published within the 3 years before the review. Abstract screening was done by one author; grey literature was excluded by the peer-review restriction; the authors judge publication bias a 'profound threat' and note that no birth cohort had reported on this question (Discussion, 4th paragraph). Two of the five reports share one cohort, so the evidence is four cohorts, not five studies.

exposure.measurement: Age of first drink of more than a few sips, self-reported prospectively in adolescence, with study-specific definitions: half a bottle of beer, 100 mL of wine or 25 mL of spirits, used as a continuous variable (Pedersen & Skrondal); a first drink before 11, separately at a family gathering or elsewhere (Warner & White); four bands, under 11, 11–14, 15–17 and 18–20, with 11–14 as reference (Guttmannova 2011), and before 11 or not (Guttmannova 2012); any drinking by 13–14, from questions about the most recent drinking occasion (Rossow & Kuntsche) (Results, 2nd to 6th paragraphs; Table 1).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable: the exposure is the age of the first drink, not amount or frequency.
exposure.polysubstance: Only the Seattle analyses adjusted for adolescent use of other substances (tobacco, marijuana and other illicit drugs in 2011; tobacco, marijuana and heavy episodic drinking in one 2012 model); the other studies did not (Table 1).

comparison.controls: Within each cohort, people who started drinking later: continuous AFD (Pedersen & Skrondal); first drink at 11 or older at a family gathering (Warner & White); first drink at 11–14 (Guttmannova 2011); first drink at 11 or older (Guttmannova 2012); no drinking by 13–14 (Rossow & Kuntsche).
comparison.matching: Not applicable at review level. Adjustment sets differ widely (Table 1): parental and peer norms and use (Pedersen & Skrondal); gender, religion, parental status, features of the first drinking episode, family history of alcoholism, family and friends' drinking, parental relationship, delinquency, school performance and psychiatric symptoms (Warner & White); gender, ethnicity, childhood poverty and adolescent substance use (Guttmannova 2011), plus parental drinking, family factors and four sets of mediators (2012); gender and conduct problems (Rossow & Kuntsche).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The review assessed control for socioeconomic status, family history of alcohol problems, mental health and early behaviour problems (Methods, 5th paragraph); only Warner & White adjusted for family history and psychiatric symptoms. No included study used a twin, sibling or adoption design, so familial and genetic liability was not controlled. The authors also raise overadjustment, for example peer variables that may lie on the causal path (Discussion, 3rd paragraph).

outcomes.instruments: As used by the primary studies (Table 1): past-month consumption and the Rutgers Alcohol Problem Index (Pedersen & Skrondal); lifetime problem drinking, abuse or dependence (Warner & White); past-year alcohol misuse and DSM-IV dependence at each wave, and the number of waves with a diagnosis (chronicity) (Guttmannova 2011, 2012); intoxication 10 or more times in the past year and an AUDIT score of 8 or more (Rossow & Kuntsche).
outcomes.validity_norms: The review judges outcome measurement reliable and generally validated (Discussion, 2nd paragraph); no formal appraisal tool was used.
outcomes.operationalization: An adult alcohol outcome was any of the measures above at 18 or older; associations were taken as reported (odds ratios, regression or structural-equation coefficients) without conversion to a common metric.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable to the narrative synthesis; 10 counts the outcome measures across the five reports in Table 1, several of them examined in more than one model.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Abstracts were screened by the first author alone; selected full texts were reviewed independently by both authors; data were extracted with a dedicated form, but who extracted them, and whether in duplicate, is not stated (Methods, 3rd and 4th paragraphs).

analysis.effect_sizes: No pooled estimate: meta-analysis was judged inappropriate because of heterogeneous methods and outcomes. Study results as reported (Table 1; Results): Pedersen & Skrondal, structural coefficients of -3.465 for alcohol debut age on consumption and -13.828 on the problem index (both p<0.0001), described as roughly a 35% reduction in consumption for a 10% delay in debut, with weak control of confounding. Warner & White, a first drink before 11 at a family gathering OR 2.39 (95% CI 1.10 to 5.20) and elsewhere OR 5.75 (1.53 to 21.54), both against a first drink at 11 or older at a family gathering, for lifetime problem drinking by 31, in a model adjusting for features of the first drink, gender, socioeconomic status and religion; in the fully adjusted model AFD was not significant (coefficient -0.0631, p>0.05), while feeling drunk at the first drink was (0.3848, p<0.0001). Guttmannova 2011, no association of AFD with alcohol misuse (ORs 0.96, 1.40 and 0.64 against 11–14, all p>0.05) or with dependence at any follow-up (1.49, 1.16 and 0.35, all p>0.05), but a first drink before 11 went with a past-year dependence diagnosis at more of the follow-up interviews (OR 1.68, p<0.05); starting regular drinking at 15–17 was consistently associated with misuse and dependence. Guttmannova 2012, early AFD and chronicity of dependence, β=0.44 (p<0.05) unadjusted and 0.45 to 0.53 in four adjusted models. Rossow & Kuntsche, drinking by 13–14 and frequent intoxication OR 1.5 (1.2 to 1.9) and AUDIT 8 or more OR 1.6 (1.3 to 2.1), adjusted for gender; after adding adolescent conduct problems, 1.2 (0.9 to 1.6) for both.
analysis.covariates: None at review level; each study's adjustment set is listed in Table 1.
analysis.preregistration_detail: The review states it is guided by PRISMA; no protocol or registration is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: Every included report's main results are summarized, including null ones. Several primary estimates are given without confidence intervals (all Seattle odds ratios and coefficients carry p-values only), and one Seattle cell (AFD 18–20, chronicity of dependence) gives a p-value without an estimate (Table 1).
analysis.power: Not addressed. Five reports of 447 to 1311 participants, with the main exposure contrasts often small subgroups (for example a first drink before 11).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Four cohorts in the USA and Norway. An earlier first drink went with adult drinking or problems in some analyses (Pedersen & Skrondal, with weak confounder control; Warner & White before full adjustment; Rossow & Kuntsche adjusted for gender only; chronicity of dependence in the Seattle cohort, which did not change across four adjusted models in the 2012 report) and not in others (misuse and any dependence in the Seattle cohort; Warner & White and Rossow & Kuntsche after broader adjustment or adjustment for conduct problems). Feeling drunk at the first drink and early regular drinking had larger associations than the age of the first drink.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that rigorous control for confounding 'markedly attenuates or eliminates any observed effects' and concludes that there is no strong evidence that starting earlier leads to adult problems, so that policy makers should reconsider delaying initiation as a strategy against adult problems. Gaps: (1) the generalization does not hold for the Seattle 2012 report, whose association with chronicity of dependence was unchanged by adjustment (β 0.44 unadjusted, 0.45 to 0.53 adjusted), and the Discussion itself notes that this report rejected a marker explanation, yet its last paragraph lists it among the studies supporting the absence of an effect; (2) a lack of strong evidence from four small cohorts, which the authors fear are distorted by publication bias, is turned into a policy recommendation that reads as evidence of no effect, while the review's own final sentence says we do not yet know; (3) the Discussion's caution that adjustment for peer variables may be overadjustment, which would make attenuation after adjustment weaker evidence of confounding, does not reach the abstract. The review is otherwise explicit about how small and uncertain the evidence base is.

timeline.event: Grant & Dawson, NLAES: the cross-sectional association between age at onset of alcohol use and DSM-IV abuse and dependence, with ages recalled in adulthood (cited by this review among the mostly cross-sectional studies behind US and UK guidance).
Prescott & Kendler, twin study: age at first drink and alcoholism, described in its title as a non-causal association (cited for the marker hypothesis).

King & Chassin, prospective study of children of alcoholics (excluded as a special population): earlier first drink unrelated to alcohol dependence after confounders were taken into account (as summarized in the Discussion).

Two NESARC analyses (Hingson et al., 2006; Dawson et al., 2008), excluded because AFD was recalled in adulthood, both found small associations of AFD with adult outcomes (as summarized in the Discussion).
This review (online November 2013): five reports from four cohorts, mixed results.

Irons, Iacono & McGue, Minnesota twin cohort (read in this round): drinking by 14 associated with the adult alcohol-use index within exposure-discordant twin pairs, including MZ pairs, attenuated but not eliminated relative to propensity-weighted estimates; no significant within-MZ-pair association with alcohol abuse or dependence symptoms.

replication.where_it_stands: The only systematic review of prospective cohorts on this question named in the round's reading list, and for alcohol only. Its core message, that prospective general-population evidence was sparse and mixed in 2013, stands; its abstract overstates how consistently adjustment removes the association. Later co-twin evidence (Irons et al., 2015) found associations of early drinking with adult alcohol use that survived control for shared familial factors, so the question remains open, as the review's own last sentence says. No later systematic review was searched here.

funding.funder: The work of the second author was supported by a Wellcome Trust Research Career Development Fellowship in Basic Biomedical Science (WT086516MA) (Footnotes, Funding).
funding.declared_conflicts: Competing interests: none. Provenance: not commissioned; externally peer reviewed.
funding.affiliations_note: The second author wrote the related review whose references were screened and which informed the design (McCambridge, McAlaney & Rowe, 2011), and the papers on publication bias cited to support the publication-bias concern (refs 25 and 26); none of the five included studies is by the review authors.

what_would_settle_it: Individual-participant analyses of several large birth or school cohorts, with the first drink recorded as it happens, harmonized adult DSM or ICD outcomes and the same confounder set, combined with designs that control familial liability (MZ twins or siblings discordant for early drinking) and with natural experiments that shift the age of first drinking for reasons unrelated to the person (for example changes in minimum legal drinking ages).

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: General-population cohorts, AFD measured in adolescence, later starters as comparators, adult alcohol outcomes, at least 3 years of follow-up.
No protocol or registration is mentioned; PRISMA guidance alone is cited.
Restriction to prospective cohorts is justified by recall and reporting bias in retrospective designs and by the scarcity of experimental data (Methods, 1st paragraph).

Four databases, a printed strategy (Box 1), no language or date limits, reference lists and forward citations searched, 20 experts contacted, search within 24 months of publication; but inclusion was limited to peer-reviewed studies without a stated justification and no grey literature was sought. Judged 'no' under the project's strict reading of item 4 (an unjustified publication restriction fails partial yes; decision p-amstar2-item4); if a peer-review restriction is not counted as a publication restriction, the item would be at least partial yes. The overall rating does not depend on it.
Abstracts were screened by the first author alone; only full texts were reviewed independently by both authors.
A dedicated extraction form was used; who extracted the data, and whether a second reviewer checked it, is not stated.

domains.note: The PRISMA flow diagram is an image (figure image not viewable); the text names a few excluded studies with reasons (refs 23, 24 and 27 to 29) but gives no list of excluded full texts.

domains.note: Table 1 gives cohort, setting, sample size, follow-up rate, timing of AFD and outcome measurement, outcomes, confounders and results; participant characteristics such as sex are not given.

domains.note: Confounding, selection, attrition, recall and exposure and outcome measurement are appraised narratively, with per-study judgments of confounder control in the Discussion; no tool, no assessment of selective reporting of results.

domains.note: Narrative synthesis; meta-analysis judged inappropriate because of heterogeneity.

13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The interpretation weights studies by their control of confounding (for example discounting Pedersen & Skrondal for weak control) and discusses overadjustment; see the reporting issue on the classification of the Seattle 2012 report.
Differences in exposure definitions, adjustment sets, samples and cultures are discussed as reasons for the mixed results.
No quantitative assessment is possible without pooling, but publication bias is discussed at length and judged a profound threat.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Three critical items are not met (no protocol; no list of excluded studies; a search limited to peer-reviewed publications without justification, under the project's strict reading of item 4), which gives critically low confidence by the AMSTAR 2 rule even without item 4. Single-reviewer abstract screening and unverified extraction add to the risk that eligible reports were missed in a field of five. The review is nonetheless careful about the limits of its evidence, restricts itself to the right design for the question, and states that the answer is unknown. Cite it for the scarcity and mixed direction of prospective general-population evidence up to January 2013 (alcohol only) and as a pointer to the five reports; do not cite its abstract's statement that adjustment eliminates the association, which one of its own included reports contradicts.

key_findings.finding: Only five reports met the criteria: three from two US cohorts and two from two Norwegian cohorts, with samples of 447 to 1311, all school- or community-based; three of them (2011 to 2013) were published within the 3 years before the review.

Search: Medline, Embase, PsycInfo and Social Policy and Practice from inception to 10 January 2013, no language or date limits, peer-reviewed studies only, with backward and forward citation searching, 20 experts contacted and a related review's references screened; abstracts screened by the first author, full texts independently by both authors.

Oslo cohort (n=522): later alcohol debut was strongly associated with lower consumption and fewer problems at 18–21 (structural coefficients -3.465 and -13.828, p<0.0001), estimated as about a 35% reduction in consumption for a 10% delay, after control for parental and peer influences only; the original authors expected stricter control to weaken it.

Rutgers cohort (n=447, completers only): a first drink before 11 went with lifetime problem drinking by 31 (at a family gathering OR 2.39, 95% CI 1.10 to 5.20; elsewhere OR 5.75, 1.53 to 21.54; both against a first drink at 11 or older at a family gathering) after adjustment for features of the first drink, gender, socioeconomic status and religion, but not after adjustment for further risk factors (coefficient -0.0631, p>0.05); feeling drunk at the first drink remained a strong predictor (0.3848, p<0.0001).

Seattle cohort, 2011 report (n=808 who started before 21): AFD was not associated with adult alcohol misuse or with any dependence to 33 (against a first drink at 11–14, for a first drink before 11, at 15–17 and at 18–20: misuse at any follow-up OR 0.96, 1.40 and 0.64; dependence at any follow-up 1.49, 1.16 and 0.35; chronicity of misuse 1.20, 1.13 and 0.77; all p>0.05), but a first drink before 11 went with a past-year dependence diagnosis at more of the follow-up interviews (every 3 years from 21 to 33) than a first drink at 11–14 (OR 1.68, p<0.05); starting regular drinking at 15–17 was consistently associated with misuse and dependence.
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph; Table 1, Guttmannova et al 2011 row
key_findings.note: No confidence intervals are given for the Seattle estimates.

key_findings.finding: Seattle cohort, 2012 report (subset of 706): a first drink before 11 was associated with chronicity of dependence (β=0.44, p<0.05), and the association was essentially unchanged in four models adding peer, school, behavioural and substance-use factors (β 0.45 to 0.53); none of the three explanations tested (confounding by other risk factors, developmental impairment, more adolescent substance use) was supported.

Young in Norway cohort (n=1311): drinking by 13–14 went with frequent intoxication (OR 1.5, 1.2 to 1.9) and AUDIT 8 or more (OR 1.6, 1.3 to 2.1) at 26–27 when adjusted for gender, and both fell to 1.2 (0.9 to 1.6) after adjustment for adolescent conduct problems.
Follow-up exceeded 80% in every included study; the authors consider selection in sample construction, not attrition, the larger threat to generalizability.

The authors judge publication bias a profound threat to any inference, noting that no birth-cohort study had reported on the question, and that the evidence comes only from high-income countries without a Mediterranean drinking culture.

Excluded studies pointing the same way: a prospective study of children of alcoholics found earlier AFD unrelated to dependence after adjustment, and two NESARC analyses with recalled AFD found small associations.
Feeling drunk at the first drinking episode and the start of regular drinking showed larger associations with adult problems than the age of the first drink itself.

The authors conclude that the sensible position is that it is not yet known whether starting to drink earlier leads to adult alcohol problems, and that prevention should be justified by the acute harms of drinking in young people.

reporting_issues.issue: The last paragraph of the Discussion lists the second Seattle report (Guttmannova et al., 2012) among the studies supporting the absence of an effect of AFD, but the review's own summary of that report says the association with chronicity of dependence was unchanged across four adjusted models and that none of the explanations tested, including confounding, was supported, and the Discussion's 7th paragraph says the report rejected a marker hypothesis.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Discussion, 10th paragraph; Results, 5th paragraph; Discussion, 7th paragraph; Table 1
reporting_issues.consequence: The tally of supporting and non-supporting studies is misstated: on the review's own summaries, two of the four cohorts show an association that survived the adjustment made (Seattle chronicity; Oslo, under weak control) and two do not.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract's Results state that rigorous control for confounding markedly attenuates or eliminates any observed effects, which is contradicted by the Seattle 2012 report (β 0.44 unadjusted, 0.45 to 0.53 adjusted) summarized in the same review.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract (Results); Results, 5th paragraph; Table 1
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract's generalization should not be cited; attenuation after adjustment was seen in two of the four cohorts.

reporting_issues.issue: The criteria require AFD measured in adolescence, with at least 3 years between the initial adolescent AFD measurement and the adult outcome, but the Seattle 2011 report's exposure bands include a first drink at 18–20 with outcomes measured from 21, Table 1 lists AFD collection in that cohort up to 27 (up to 24 in the 2012 report) overlapping the outcome waves, and the Oslo cohort charted AFD up to the outcome wave (18–21).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods, 2nd paragraph; Results, 2nd and 4th paragraphs; Table 1
reporting_issues.consequence: The 3-year rule applies to the first wave of AFD measurement, not to each person's first drink; for late starters in two of the four cohorts the first drink was neither adolescent nor 3 years before the outcome, which weakens the protection against recall and reverse timing that the review claims for its design.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives a follow-up rate of 100% for the Seattle 2012 report, which analysed a subset of 706 from a cohort reported as 808 in the 2011 report.
reporting_issues.consequence: The 100% describes an analytic subset rather than retention; about 13% of the earlier analytic sample is not in it (editors' arithmetic). It does not change the review's conclusions.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract counts 'five studies', but two of the five reports come from the same Seattle cohort.
reporting_issues.consequence: The evidence base is four independent cohorts; claims should say so.
